# `\textcolor{pmxgreen}{(pmxhelpr)}`{=latex} Function Friday
:::

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
```

The dose-proportionality assessment toolchain  within `pmxhelpr`
consists of a summary function, `df_doseprop()`, and a dual-mode plotting 
function, `plot_doseprop()`, mirroring the architecture of the VPC toolchain.
The summary `doseprop_stats`object contains the tabulated power law regression
statistics. The plotting function can perform one-step summary statistic 
calculation and plotting, or use a precomputed `vpc_stats` object in a two-step
workflow.

Dose proportionality assessment evaluates whether exposure increases 
proportionally with dose. The standard approach to this assessment is power law 
regression on the relationship

$$Exposure = \alpha \cdot DOSE^\gamma$$

which linearizes via log transformation to

$$\log(Exposure) = intercept + \gamma \cdot \log(DOSE)$$

Hypothesis testing proceeds via the confidence interval around the power 
estimate ($\gamma$): the null is dose-proportional ($\gamma = 1$); the 
alternative is non-proportional ($\gamma \ne 1$). Interpretation rules of thumb:

  + CI includes 1: dose-proportional
  + CI excludes 1, upper bound below 1: less than dose-proportional
  + CI excludes 1, lower bound above 1: greater than dose-proportional

This assessment is typically performed single dose Cmax and AUC using data from
the first-in-human (FIH) study. The combination assessment of these metrics 
informs which phase of the PK profile is contributing most to non-linearity 
(e.g., absorption rate [Ka], absorption extent [F], or elimination [CL]). 

# Example Analysis Dataset: `data_sad_nca`

The `data_sad_nca` dataset internal to `pmxhelpr` contains NCA parameters
for the `data_sad` SAD and FE first-in-human (FIH) study. The dataset is 
formatted following SDTM `PP` (Pharmacokinetic Parameters) domain conventions. 

We will filter to common dose administration conditions in the fasted state in 
Part 1 of the study, to avoid confounding the assessment of dose-proportionality
with the effect of food.

```{r data-prep}
data_nca1 <- filter(data_sad_nca, PART == "Part 1-SAD")
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Dose-proportionality Assessment Tabulation: `df_doseprop()`

The `df_doseprop()` function performs the log-log regression of exposure 
metrics vs dose and returns an object with the summary statistics. 

There are two required arguments:

  + `data` — a `data.frame` of NCA parameters
  + `metrics` — character vector of exposure metric names in `data` to evaluate
  
Additional optional arguments must be specified if different from SDTM.PP
formatting specifications:

  + `metric_name_var`: variable in `data` containing metric names requested in
      `metrics`, default `PPTESTCD`.
  + `metric_value_var`: variable in `data` containing exposure metric values, 
      default `PPORRES`.
    
The default argument for the numeric dose variable `dose_var` is `DOSE`.
  
```{r df-doseprop-obj}
dose_prop_obj <- df_doseprop(data_nca1, metrics = c("aucinf.obs", "cmax"))
dose_prop_obj
```
The returned `doseprop_stats` S3 class object provides a nice print summary of
the dimensions of the stats data.frame, configuration details, a succinct 
summary of the `stats` data.frame, and a note that the input dataset is retained
for plotting. 

The `stats` slot holds the per-metric estimates from the log-log regression, 
which contains all the information needed to format an output table.

{{< pagebreak >}}

Additional arguments to `df_doseprop()` control options within the log-log
regression.

  + `method`: distribution used to calculate the confidence interval. Default is
    `"normal"`. Alternative `"tdist"` may be preferred for small samples size 
    where normality cannot be assumed (e.g, < 30).
  + `ci`: confidence interval to return expressed as a proportion. Default is 
    `"0.9"` based on the CI recommended for the bioequivalence assessment.
  + `sigdigits`: number of significant digits to return in outputs
  
This example modifies the method from the normal distribution assumptions to 
the t-distribution and requests the 95% CI with 2 significant digits.
  
```{r df-doseprop-obj-95ci-tdist}
dose_prop_obj_tdist <- df_doseprop(data_nca1,metrics = c("aucinf.obs", "cmax"), 
                                        method = "tdist", 
                                        ci = 0.95, sigdigits = 2)
```

Let's render the stats elements using `gt()` to compare estimates.

```{r table-norm-dist}
dose_prop_obj$stats %>% select(-Intercept, -StandardError) %>% gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Dose-proportionality Assessment (Part 1-SAD)", 
             subtitle = "Normal Distribution | 90% CI") %>%
  tab_options(latex.use_longtable = TRUE,table.font.size = px(10),
              heading.title.font.size = px(14), 
              heading.subtitle.font.size = px(14))
```

```{r table-tdist}
dose_prop_obj_tdist$stats %>% select(-Intercept, -StandardError) %>% gt() %>%
  tab_header(title = "Dose-proportionality Assessment (Part 1-SAD)", 
             subtitle = "t-Distribution | 95% CI") %>%
  tab_options(latex.use_longtable = TRUE,table.font.size = px(10),
              heading.title.font.size = px(14), 
              heading.subtitle.font.size = px(14))
```
